script.text: About one barrel of oil in every five that the world uses normally passes through a gap of water just twenty-one miles wide. Since the war with Iran began in February, ship traffic there has fallen sharply, according to the British monitoring center UKMTO. So why does one strait matter so much?

Why can't ships simply go around this strait? Who depends on its oil and gas? What can the escape routes really carry? And what has happened since the war began in February? There is one number that shows how far the International Energy Agency's largest-ever stock release goes.

The Strait of Hormuz sits between Iran in the north and Oman in the south. It connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, and from there to the Arabian Sea. At its narrowest, the strait is about twenty-one miles wide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. But ships cannot use all of that. The agency adds that traffic moves in two lanes, each about two miles wide, one inbound and one outbound, with a two-mile buffer between them. Iran holds the entire northern shore. Why does that matter? Because the oil and gas ports of Kuwait, Qatar and southern Iraq all sit inside the Gulf. So do the main terminals of Saudi Arabia and the Emirates. According to the agency, about twenty million barrels of oil moved through the strait every day in twenty twenty-four. That was roughly a fifth of everything the world consumed. The International Energy Agency puts its twenty twenty-five figure at the same level, about a quarter of all oil traded by sea. Count crude alone, and the agency's twenty twenty-six factsheet says nearly fifteen million barrels a day crossed in twenty twenty-five, about a third of all crude traded worldwide.

Now, who is on the other end? Mostly Asia. The Energy Information Administration estimates that eighty-four percent of the crude oil and condensate that crossed the strait in twenty twenty-four went to Asian markets. China, India, Japan and South Korea alone took sixty-nine percent. The International Energy Agency says China and India together received forty-four percent of the crude that crossed in twenty twenty-five. The Energy Information Administration calls Hormuz the world's most important oil transit chokepoint. Then there is gas. Qatar is the world's second largest exporter of liquefied natural gas, and the agency says about ninety-three percent of it leaves through Hormuz. Together, Qatar and the Emirates supply about nineteen percent of global liquefied natural gas trade, and almost all of it passes through the strait. The Energy Information Administration also estimates that eighty-three percent of the liquefied gas moving through the strait in twenty twenty-four went to Asian buyers. Quick question: what share of all of Asia's liquefied natural gas imports came through this strait in twenty twenty-five? Take a guess. About twenty-seven percent, according to the agency. More than a quarter of Asia's liquefied gas imports, through one narrow strait.

So can the Gulf simply go around? Partly. Two pipelines matter most. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline carries crude across the kingdom to Yanbu, on the Red Sea. The U.S. Energy Information Administration put its capacity at five million barrels a day in twenty twenty-three. Bloomberg reported in March that Saudi Arabia was running it at about seven million, above that earlier rating. The second route belongs to the Emirates. Its Abu Dhabi crude oil pipeline runs to Fujairah, on the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait. The National and Reuters put its capacity between one point five and one point eight million barrels a day. Iran has its own small line, from Goreh to Jask, also outside the strait. The agency gives it an effective capacity of about three hundred thousand barrels a day. Before the war, the U.S. agency estimated that only about two point six million barrels a day of bypass capacity was actually spare, because the pipelines already carried oil in normal times. Set that against the twenty million that normally sail through. By simple arithmetic, it covers about one eighth. The International Energy Agency uses a wider range for all bypass routes together, three and a half to five and a half million barrels a day. Even its top number is far below normal flows. And the workarounds carry their own risks. The Oil and Gas Journal reported that Fujairah was hit by several attacks in April, which the Emirates blamed on Iran. Seatrade Maritime reported that Iran struck the pipeline feeding Yanbu that same month. And in the summer, Gulf News reported, the Houthis in Yemen declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The National reports that the Emirates is now building a second pipeline to double its capacity, expected in twenty twenty-seven.

What happened after the war began? On February twenty-eighth, the United States and Israel first struck Iran, according to ABC News. By March eleventh, Qatar's liquefied natural gas production was curtailed and force majeure had been declared on deliveries, according to the research group EPRINC. Pulse reported in late April that daily crossings had fallen from about one hundred thirty ships to about seven. It has not been a clean shutdown. Iran's foreign minister said Iran briefly reopened the strait in April, at Pakistan's request, according to ARY News. In June, InvestingLive reported that Iran had agreed to a maritime security mechanism. Then came renewed fighting, Reuters reported, as the June interim deal faltered. In August, UKMTO said that transits were roughly ninety percent below pre-conflict levels. Today the numbers are hard to pin down. The Straits Daily Brief, citing the International Monetary Fund's PortWatch monitor, reported about four transits on October eighteenth. Lloyd's List counted at least one hundred four vessels in the week of October fifth. Different trackers, different definitions. UKMTO has said that many attacked ships never report. Last week, according to CBS News, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed to have hit seven commercial vessels. President Trump called those hits fake. CBS News said independent confirmation was not available. CBS News also reported that Brent crude briefly topped one hundred seventeen dollars. Meanwhile, Reuters reported that Pakistan's army chief visited Tehran, where Iran's president said Washington must lift sanctions and end its threats before any talks.

So what happens next? Start with the stockpile. In March, the thirty-two member countries of the International Energy Agency agreed to release four hundred million barrels from emergency reserves, the largest release in the agency's history. Do the simple arithmetic: divide that by the twenty million barrels that normally pass through the strait each day, and it covers about twenty days. That is the number: about twenty days of Hormuz oil. The trade outlet Engine reported in October that about three hundred thirty million barrels had been drawn, The agency's chief, Fatih Birol, has said, according to Business Today, that it can release more if needed. He has called the release a buffer, not a lasting solution. In August, the U.S. agency raised its Brent forecast to eighty-seven dollars a barrel for the year, citing Hormuz shipping constraints. Beyond stocks, three developments are reported. The first is price. Earlier this year, Fitch said Brent could average one hundred twenty dollars if the strait stays effectively closed for six months. The second path is diplomacy. Pakistan is pressing for a deal to reopen the strait, and Iran says it wants sanctions lifted first. The third path is renewed war. Al Jazeera, citing The New York Times, reported that American and Israeli officials are drawing up options for new strikes, with a possible window in early November, but no decision has been made. Will shipping through the strait return to normal levels before the end of the year? Tell us in the comments: yes or no.
Next: the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia's escape route ends in waters the Houthis say they are blockading. Who are the Houthis, and how did a rebel group threaten one of the world's busiest shipping lanes?

upload.title: The 21-Mile Strait Behind a Fifth of the World's Oil
upload.description:
About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, a gap between Iran and Oman roughly 21 miles wide at its narrowest. This explainer shows where the strait is, who depends on its oil and gas, what the bypass pipelines can really carry, what has happened to shipping since the war with Iran began on February 28, 2026, and what sources and analysts say could come next. Claims are attributed to their sources; disputed or unverified claims are labelled.
